slides.heading: Find Successor
slides.subtitle: AlgoExpert · Medium · Binary Trees
slides.narration: Let's solve Find Successor, a medium binary trees problem. We'll restate the problem, build the intuition, walk through the approach, read the Java solution, and finish with its complexity.

slides.heading: The problem
bullets: Nodes have parent pointers; return the in-order successor of `node` (or null).
slides.narration: Here's the problem. Nodes have parent pointers; return the in-order successor of node (or null).

slides.heading: Intuition
bullets: The in-order successor is the leftmost node of the right subtree, or else the first ancestor reached from a left child.
slides.narration: The in-order successor is the leftmost node of the right subtree, or else the first ancestor reached from a left child.

slides.heading: Brute force vs optimal
bullets: In-order traversal into a list, find node, take next → O(n)
Parent pointers: two cases → O(h) time, O(1) space
slides.narration: The simple approach does a full in-order traversal and returns the next element, linear time and space. With parent pointers, we only need two cases, costing at most the tree's height and constant space.

slides.heading: Approach
bullets: 1. If there's a right subtree, go right then all the way left
2. Otherwise climb parents until we come from a left child
slides.narration: Step by step. First, if there's a right subtree, go right then all the way left. Second, otherwise climb parents until we come from a left child.

slides.heading: Worked example
slides.caption: Successor of 5: no right child
slides.narration: Find the in-order successor of five. Five has no right child, so the successor is above it.

slides.heading: Worked example
slides.caption: 5 is 2's RIGHT child → keep climbing
slides.narration: Five is its parent two's right child, so two comes before it. Keep climbing.

slides.heading: Worked example
slides.caption: 2 is 1's LEFT child → successor is 1
slides.narration: Two is the left child of one, so one is the successor.

slides.heading: Worked example
slides.caption: Successor of 1: leftmost of right subtree → 3
slides.narration: For node one, which has a right subtree, the successor is the leftmost node of that subtree: three.

slides.heading: Java solution
slides.narration: If the node has a right child, we go right once and then all the way left. Otherwise we climb while the current node is its parent's right child and return the parent, which is null if we ran off the top.

slides.heading: Complexity
slides.narration: Time is O of h. Space is constant.

slides.heading: Edge cases & pitfalls
bullets: Node with right subtree → leftmost of it
Climb while we're a right child
slides.narration: The last node in order has no successor, so return null. Climb only while the current node is its parent's right child.

slides.heading: Interview tips & follow-ups
bullets: Follow-up: without parent pointers in a BST
slides.narration: The predecessor is the mirror image. In a BST without parent pointers, search from the root tracking the last left turn.

slides.heading: Recap
bullets: The in-order successor is the leftmost node of the right subtree, or else the first ancestor reached from a left child.
slides.narration: To recap Find Successor: The in-order successor is the leftmost node of the right subtree, or else the first ancestor reached from a left child. Try re-implementing it from scratch without looking.
